methodology: Provenance-preserving reconciliation of previously screened PR #290. Not new screening. Unverified candidate passages are not publication-ready. Critical-text, manuscript, and canonical-ledger union pending.

records.topic: Do not turn backs when meeting opposing forces in battle

unverified_research_leads.difference: Deuteronomy exhorts Israel not to fear a superior enemy because God accompanies them; it does not formulate the Qur'anic prohibition on turning away.

records.pending_question: Check Hebrew Deut 20 in context and distinguish generic military exhortation from a source-specific textual parallel.

records.topic: Exceptions for tactical maneuver or joining another unit; divine displeasure for desertion

unverified_research_leads.difference: Deuteronomy lists pre-battle exemptions and dismissal of the fearful; the Qur'an discusses turning away during an encounter and explicit tactical exceptions.

records.pending_question: Compare military law genres and historical contexts; this is a contrast, not an identified antecedent.

records.topic: God rather than the believers is credited with killing; God rather than Muhammad with throwing

unverified_research_leads.difference: David declares the battle belongs to the LORD and that victory does not depend on sword or spear; the Qur'an includes the distinctive address about throwing, absent from 1 Samuel.

records.pending_question: Verify Hebrew wording and investigate whether any securely pre-Islamic text contains a distinctive divine-throwing formulation; do not conflate Badr narrative traditions with earlier sources.
Generic divine frustration of hostile schemes is widespread; no distinctive earlier passage established.

records.topic: Appeal for decision or victory; warning against renewed conflict; assurance that numbers will not help

unverified_research_leads.difference: Jonathan says the LORD can save by many or by few; Qur'an 8:19 addresses the adversaries and warns that their multitude will not avail them.

records.pending_question: Check translation of istiftah and classical Badr context separately; do not assume direct textual borrowing.
